questions.note: Order reads right: hallux longest and broad, the 2nd a few mm short, 3–5 stepping down, the 5th rolled outward. Individuality is weak: toes 3–4 are plump smooth cylinders with soft knuckles, almost no DIP and only a few shallow wrinkle strokes; the 5th sits beside the 4th instead of under it; from below the creases are straight cuts. Toe 2's knuckle and the hallux pulp are the best.

All five nails sit in folds with visible free-edge thickness and a hallux lunula; none floats or sinks, and the hallux is cut near straight. But they read as a fresh pedicure: even pale glossy pink, crisp white French-tip edges, no ridging, yellowing, thickening or grime; nails 2–4 are near copies and the 5th a small replica, not a thick ridged nail; lateral folds are thin lines.

Tendons do read as relief that catches light: the EDL fan in V1f and V5f, a cord along the medial dorsum in V2. But they are thin, even and parallel, running at full strength to the webs, the EHL no stronger than the rest. No vein shows anywhere: no dorsal venous arch over the metatarsals, no great saphenous in front of the medial malleolus.

SSS is restrained: toe shadow sides stay dark, nothing glows. But the skin reads as clean silicone: one cloudy mottle everywhere, no redness at knuckles or nail folds, toes smooth and faintly rubbery in V5f with no cells or pores; cells show only in the hr closeups. Pad ridges are perfect target whorls and corduroy with a seam; the heel callus is a crackle decal.

defects.what: The whole plantar heel pad is capped by pale crackle callus that ends on a hard straight line across the heel, like a decal edge; the pad centre reads as cracked crust instead of thick, pink-blended weight-bearing skin.
defects.fix: Real heel callus is a 12–18 mm band on the posterior-lateral rim with a feathered edge; the pad's centre is thick, pressure-pink skin, not crust.

defects.what: Medial view: from heel to ball the medial border sits only a few mm off the floor and the dorsum is a straight ramp; the longitudinal arch and the navicular bump barely read, so the foot looks flat-footed.
defects.fix: A fit man's standing foot lifts its medial border clearly between heel and ball, with the navicular tuberosity a small dome near z 42 and a convex instep.

defects.what: No veins anywhere: no great saphenous in front of the medial malleolus, no dorsal venous arch or tributaries over the metatarsals (V1f, V2); the foot reads bloodless next to the anchor's men's feet.
defects.fix: On a lean man the dorsal venous arch and the great saphenous stand 0.7–1 mm proud, 2.5–3.5 mm wide, faintly blue-grey, and catch the rim light.

defects.what: The heel callus crack pattern is a fine, even Voronoi mesh of thin dark lines on grey-cream, reading as dried mud or crackle glaze, with a sharp top boundary.
defects.fix: Real heel callus is yellow-white and thick, fading into the skin, split by a few deeper fissures running across the rim edge, not an even polygon mesh.

defects.what: Nails 2–4 are near-identical rounded tombstones of uniform pale glossy pink with a crisp white French-tip line, and the 5th is a small copy of them; they read as copy-pasted press-ons.
defects.fix: Real lesser nails differ per toe in shape and curvature, with faint yellowing, ridges, slightly ragged trimmed edges and grime beneath; the 5th is small, thick and ridged.

defects.what: The hallux nail reads as a fresh pedicure: one even pale pink, glossy, whiter than the skin even at native size, a clean grey free edge, no ridges, no yellowing, no grime under the edge.
defects.fix: A 40-year-old soldier's hallux nail is thicker, faintly ivory-yellow and less glossy, with fine longitudinal ridges, a slightly irregular edge and dark debris under it.

defects.what: The lesser toes are smooth plump cylinders: soft PIP knuckles, almost no DIP, one or two shallow wrinkles, no redness or darkening over the joints and little curl; they read young and soft.
defects.fix: Boot-wearer's toes are knobbly: defined PIP knuckles with bunched, darker, redder skin and 3–6 wrinkles, a visible DIP, curled so the knuckles rise and the tips tuck down.

defects.what: The instep and metatarsal dorsum carry no hair at all; only the hallux and toes 2–4 have a few, so the foot looks shaved next to the anchor's men's feet.
defects.fix: Sparse dark terminal hairs, about 2 per cm² and 6–10 mm long, lie flat toward the toes over the dorsum, thinning toward the toes.

defects.what: From behind, the Achilles is a faint ridge in a broad, smooth column; the retro-malleolar hollows barely show, so the back of the ankle reads padded rather than lean.
defects.fix: The Achilles is a distinct cord about 16 mm wide and 7 mm proud, with 4 mm hollows either side between it and the malleoli.

defects.what: Lateral view: the lateral malleolus reads only as a soft broad swelling, with no crisp bony knob and no hollow in front of or behind it; the outer ankle looks smooth and puffy.
defects.fix: The lateral malleolus is a distinct 24 mm dome about 5 mm proud, lower and further back than the medial, with the sinus-tarsi hollow in front and a groove behind.

defects.what: No callus where boots wear a soldier's foot: none under the 1st–2nd MT heads, on the lateral 5th MTP or the medial hallux IP, and no corn on toe 4's PIP; only the heel has any.
defects.fix: A boot-wearing foot has paler, drier, rougher callus at the ball (32 x 22 mm), the lateral 5th MTP (18 mm) and the medial hallux IP (14 x 10 mm), and often a small corn on a lesser toe's PIP.

defects.what: Plantar friction ridges are too perfect: concentric target whorls on every toe pad and even corduroy lines over the ball, one pitch and depth everywhere, no pores, ridge breaks or crossing creases.
defects.fix: Real plantar ridges vary in pattern per pad, break and fork, carry pores along the crests, flatten under callus and are crossed by fine flexion and dryness lines.

defects.what: Thin, jagged outline lines trace the base of each toe on the sole, like a mask boundary or a torn paper edge, with a slight colour step across them.
defects.fix: The toe-base sulcus is a soft curved fold with shading, with no outline.

defects.what: The plantar flexion creases on toes 3–4 and the lines where the toes meet are razor-straight dark slits, like cuts across the toe, with no fold either side.
defects.fix: Flexion creases curve with the toe's cross-section, about 0.5 mm deep, the skin rolling into them; where toes touch, the skin flattens and bulges against its neighbour.

defects.what: The extensor tendons are thin, evenly spaced parallel ridges running at full strength right down to the webs; the EHL to the hallux is no stronger than the slips to toes 2–5.
defects.fix: The EHL is the broadest cord (5 mm, 1.5 mm proud); the EDL slips are thinner and fade toward the MTPs.

defects.what: Toe 5 sits beside toe 4 as a separate small toe at the same level, rather than tucked partly under it.
defects.fix: A real 5th toe rolls and tucks against and slightly under the 4th, its nail facing up and outward.

defects.what: The lateral border is a smooth featureless curve, with no 5th metatarsal styloid bump at mid-foot.
defects.fix: The styloid is a sharp 8 mm bump about 2.5 mm proud on the lateral border near half the foot's length.

defects.what: A thin straight seam runs from the base of the hallux pad into the whorl's centre; the ridges break and misalign across it.
defects.fix: Ridges flow continuously around the whorl's core; no line runs through it.

defects.what: The hallux tuft is a tight clump of short, straight dark strokes, some crossing at angles, reading as scratches rather than hairs lying toward the tip.
defects.fix: 8–12 slightly curved hairs, 5–8 mm long, spread over a 12 x 10 mm patch, lying flat toward the tip.

defects.what: The hallux nail's lateral folds are thin lines, so the plate looks laid on the toe rather than tucked under rolled skin; the lunula is a hard bright white crescent.
defects.fix: Lateral folds about 1 mm wide roll over the plate's edges, and the lunula is a soft milky crescent fading into the bed.

ranked: Overall the foot reads young, soft and unused, a foot model's or a mannequin's rather than a forty-year-old's who lives in boots: every surface is clean and even, nothing is worn, reddened, thickened or marked. The anchor's men's feet all show their use.

[D1] From below, the whole heel pad wears a pale crackle cap that ends on a dead-straight line across the heel, an obvious texture edge (V4). Real heel callus is a rim band with a feathered edge; the pad's centre is thick, pinkish skin.

[D2] From the medial side the foot is nearly flat: the medial border hangs a few mm over the floor from heel to ball and the instep is a straight ramp (V2). A fit man's standing foot shows a clear arch and the navicular bump.

[D3] No veins anywhere: no dorsal venous arch over the metatarsals, no great saphenous in front of the medial malleolus. On a lean forty-year-old they stand out as raised blue-grey cords, as on most of the anchor's feet.

[D4] The callus crack pattern is an even mesh of fine dark polygons on grey-cream, like dried mud or crackle glaze, with a sharp top edge (V8, V2, V3). Real heel callus is yellow-white, fades into the skin and splits in a few deep fissures across the rim.

[D5] Nails 2–4 are near-identical rounded tombstones of pale glossy pink with a white French-tip line, and the 5th is a small copy: copy-pasted press-ons. Real lesser toenails differ toe to toe, are thicker and ridged, often yellowed, the 5th small and misshapen.
[D6] The hallux nail reads as a fresh pedicure: one even pale pink, glossy, whiter than the skin even at native size (V1f), a clean grey free edge, no ridges, yellowing or grime under the edge.

[D7] The lesser toes are plump smooth cylinders with soft knuckles, almost no DIP, a few shallow wrinkle strokes, no redness over the joints and little curl. A boot-wearer's toes are knobbly, creased, ruddy at the knuckles and curled.
[D8] The instep and metatarsal dorsum are hairless while the toes carry a few hairs, so the foot looks shaved; men's feet, as in the anchor, carry sparse dark hairs lying toward the toes there.
[D9] From behind, the Achilles is only a faint ridge in a broad smooth column with shallow hollows either side (V8); a lean soldier's Achilles stands out as a cord with deep pre-Achilles hollows.
[D10] From the side the lateral malleolus is a soft swelling, not a bony knob with a hollow in front and behind (V3); the outside of the ankle reads padded.
[D11] Only the heel carries callus: none under the 1st–2nd metatarsal heads, on the lateral 5th MTP or on the medial hallux IP, and no corn on toe 4's PIP, all places boots mark a soldier's foot.

The skin's colour variation is one cloudy noise of pale and darker blobs at a single scale over the whole foot (V3, V2), with no regional logic: no redness at knuckles, toe tips and nail folds, no dusky heel sides.

[D12] The plantar ridges are too perfect: concentric target whorls on every toe pad and even corduroy lines across the ball, one pitch and depth everywhere, no pores, forks or crossing creases; they read as an engraved pattern.
[D13] Thin, jagged outline lines trace each toe's base on the sole like a mask edge or torn paper (hr.plantar); the real toe sulcus is a soft fold.
[D14] The plantar creases on toes 3–4 and the lines where the toes meet are razor-straight dark slits, like cuts, with no fold either side; real flexion creases curve round the toe and roll the skin.

[D15] The extensor tendons are thin, evenly spaced parallel ridges running at full strength down to the webs, the EHL no stronger than the slips to toes 2–5; real ones fade toward the MTPs and the EHL dominates.
At V5f's 15 px/mm the toes look smooth and faintly rubbery: no cell network, pores or dry flaking on the dorsum or the pulps; micro-relief shows only in the hr closeups.
The front of the ankle is smooth: no anterior ankle crease and none of the fine parallel lines above it (V1f, V2), which a real adult ankle shows at rest.
[D16] Toe 5 sits beside toe 4 as a separate small toe at the same level, instead of tucking partly under it.
[D17] The lateral border lacks the 5th metatarsal styloid bump at mid-foot, so the outer edge is a featureless curve (V3).
[D18] A thin straight seam runs into the hallux pad's whorl centre, the ridges breaking across it.
[D19] The hallux tuft is a tight clump of short straight dark strokes, some crossing, that reads as scratches rather than hairs lying toward the tip.
[D20] The hallux nail's lateral folds are thin lines, so the plate looks laid on top rather than tucked under rolled skin; the lunula is a hard bright crescent.
